sections.title: Sound needs a medium to propagate
Graphical Representation of a Sound Wave
Amplitude and intensity of the sound waves

slides.title: Meet the tuning fork
bullets: A tuning fork is a U-shaped metal bar with a stem, usually made of steel or aluminium.
The two sides of the U are called prongs or tines.
Striking a prong on a soft pad makes the fork vibrate and produce sound.
slides.note: Stem pakdo, pad pe gently tap karo.

slides.title: Vibration makes sound
bullets: Strike a prong gently on a rubber pad and bring the fork near your ear: you hear a sound.
Touch a water surface with a vibrating prong and waves form on the surface of the water.
The waves show the prongs are vibrating, so sound is produced by vibrating objects.

items: Strike a prong on the rubber pad
Bring the fork close to your ear
Touch still water with a prong
Watch waves spread on the water

slides.note: Take care not to strike the fork on a hard surface.

slides.title: Sound in every direction
bullets: Bring the vibrating prongs near your ear in different orientations and you still hear the sound.
This shows sound leaves the fork in multiple directions, not just one.
The directions in which sound propagates may depend on the shape of the source.
slides.note: In a village near Shillong in Meghalaya, the Whistling Village, every person has a unique tune name.

slides.title: Sound crosses the desk
slides.kicker: Ear on the table hears more
bullets: A friend gently knocks or scratches on a desk while you listen with your ear in the air.
Now place your ear against the desk, close your other ear, and listen again to the same knock.
You hear the sound through the table, so sound can travel through solids.

items: Listen with your ear in the air
Place your ear against the desk
Hear the knock through the solid table

slides.note: Solids bhi sound le jaate hain.

slides.title: Spoons under water
slides.kicker: A tap that swims to you
bullets: Tap two metal spoons against one another in air and listen to the sound they make.
Submerge the spoons in a bucket of water without touching the sides or bottom, then tap them again.
You still hear the sound, so it reached you after travelling through water and then air.

right.title: Under water
items: Sound travels through a liquid too

slides.note: Keep the spoons away from the bucket walls.

slides.title: Medium and vacuum
bullets: The material through which sound propagates is called a medium.
Sound propagates from its source to you through a medium, which can be a solid, a liquid or a gas.
A space where there is no medium (matter) is called a vacuum. Would you hear sound there?
slides.note: Hold that question for the bell jar.

slides.title: The bell jar test
bullets: An electric bell kept in a bell jar is switched on and the loudness of its sound is noted.
As air is sucked out of the jar using a vacuum pump, the sound becomes fainter.
Once near vacuum is reached, almost no sound is heard even though the bell can be seen ringing.
slides.note: Eyes see it, ears hear almost nothing.

slides.title: Air back, sound back
bullets: When air is let back into the jar, the sound can be heard again and gradually becomes as loud as before.
This experiment shows that sound cannot propagate in vacuum.
Sound needs a medium to propagate, and that medium can be a solid, a liquid or a gas.

items: Let air back into the jar
It gradually becomes as loud as before

slides.title: Silence in space
bullets: Outer space has a near vacuum, so sound cannot propagate there.
Astronauts in spacesuits cannot directly hear each other speak or hear metal objects clanking together.
Instead, they communicate through special devices fitted into their spacesuits.
slides.note: No air up there, no direct chat.

slides.title: Which way does it go
bullets: You could hear the vibrating tuning fork held near your ear in different orientations.
This indicates that sound propagates in multiple directions from the source.
For simplicity, we will consider and illustrate sound as moving in only one direction.

slides.title: Slinky push and pull
bullets: Give a stretched slinky a sharp push towards your friend and pull it back: a disturbance moves along it.
Push and pull repeatedly and a series of disturbances travels across the length of the slinky.
You see regions where the turns are closer together than usual and regions where they are more spread out.

items: Turns bunch up and spread out
Repeat for a series of disturbances

slides.note: The push-pull is like sound produced continuously.

slides.title: The mark stays put
bullets: The marked turn does not travel along the slinky; it only oscillates about its position of rest.
Each turn oscillates about its own position while the disturbance travels from one end to the other.
Closeness or spreading of turns represents the higher or lower density of air as sound travels.

items: Mark one turn with a marker
Push and pull the end of the slinky
The mark only oscillates in place
The disturbance travels the whole length

slides.note: Like the mark, air particles stay near home.

slides.title: Make grains dance
bullets: Stretch a cellophane or rubber sheet tightly over a wide mouthed container and sprinkle grains on it.
Produce a loud sound nearby using a metal plate and a beater, without touching the container.
The grains on the sheet move and jump even though nothing touched the container.

items: Stretch the sheet over the container

slides.note: Try louder and softer strikes to compare.

slides.title: Sound is energy
bullets: As sound propagates through air it reaches the sheet and makes it vibrate; this vibration moves the grains.
Sound is a form of energy: when the source vibrates, it transfers energy to the surrounding medium.
Vibrations of the medium's particles and their collisions transfer energy along; the energy travels, not the particles.

slides.title: Microphone and speaker
bullets: A microphone captures sound and converts sound energy to electrical energy as the wave passes through it.
A speaker does the opposite: an electrical signal makes its cone or diaphragm vibrate and produce sound.
If all components work properly, the sound from the speaker closely matches the originally captured sound.

slides.title: Plot the density wave
bullets: At any given instant, the density of the medium varies periodically with distance from the source.
Plot distance on the x-axis and density of the medium on the y-axis; a dashed line marks the average density.
The curve rises above and falls below the average density as you move along the distance axis.
slides.note: The dashed line is the average density.

slides.title: Crests and troughs
bullets: In a compression the density rises above the average, and the highest point of the graph is the maximum density.
Thereafter the density falls below the average in the region of rarefaction, and the lowest point is the minimum density.
The highest point is called the crest and the lowest point is called the trough of the wave.
slides.note: Crest means crowded, trough means thinned out.

slides.title: Time instead of distance
bullets: Another way to represent a sound wave is to plot the variation of density of the medium with time.
For this graph you stay at one particular location in the medium and watch the density change there.

left.title: Density vs distance
items: Crests and troughs along the path

slides.title: Wavelength
bullets: The wavelength of a wave is the distance between two consecutive crests or two consecutive troughs.
It is usually represented by the Greek letter lambda, and its SI unit is the metre (m).
Sound waves can have long wavelengths or short wavelengths.
slides.note: Crest to crest or trough to trough, same length.

slides.title: Frequency
bullets: At a fixed point, density changes from maximum to minimum and back to maximum, making one complete oscillation.
The number of density oscillations at a fixed point per unit time is the frequency of the sound wave.
Frequency is represented by the Greek letter nu; its SI unit is per second, also called the hertz (Hz).

items: Watch one fixed point in the medium
Oscillations per unit time give frequency

slides.title: Time period
bullets: The time taken for one complete density oscillation at a fixed point is the time period, represented by T.
Its SI unit is the second (s).
Time period and frequency are inversely related: T = 1/nu, so a shorter time period means a higher frequency.
slides.note: Double the frequency, halve the time period.

slides.title: Notes climb a ladder
bullets: Usually, everyday sounds contain a mixture of many frequencies.
Nearly single frequency sounds can be made by striking a tuning fork or by oral whistling.
With a frequency app, the notes Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni show frequency is lowest for Sa and gradually increases.

items: Sing or play Sa Re Ga Ma

slides.title: Amplitude of a wave
bullets: Sound propagates as density oscillations of the medium via compressions and rarefactions.
The amplitude is the maximum change in the density of air in a compression or a rarefaction compared to the average density.
A larger change in density corresponds to a larger amplitude.
slides.note: Think of the two curves in Fig 10.20.

slides.title: Bigger swing, more energy
bullets: A wave with a larger amplitude carries more energy than one with a smaller amplitude.
Strike the plate harder and more energy is transferred to the particles of the surrounding medium.
They move with larger displacements, the sheet vibrates to a larger displacement, and the grains jump higher.
slides.note: Amplitude aur energy saath badhte hain.

slides.title: Intensity fades out
bullets: Intensity is the amount of sound energy passing through a unit area perpendicular to the propagation direction in unit time.
As sound travels away from a point source it spreads over a larger area, and energy conservation spreads the same energy wider.
So intensity decreases with distance; larger amplitude sounds carry more energy and travel farther before intensity reduces to zero.
slides.note: Farther from the source, softer it sounds.

flashcards.front: What is a tuning fork?
flashcards.back: A U-shaped metal bar with a stem, usually made of steel or aluminium, struck on a pad to make it vibrate.

flashcards.front: What are the sides of a tuning fork's U called?
flashcards.back: They are called prongs or tines; striking them on a pad makes the fork vibrate.

flashcards.front: What do ripples on water touched by a tuning fork prong show?
flashcards.back: The prongs are indeed vibrating, supporting the idea that sound is produced by vibrating objects.

flashcards.front: What is special about the Whistling Village near Shillong?
flashcards.back: In that village in Meghalaya, every person has a unique tune name that can be sung or whistled.

flashcards.front: What is a medium in the study of sound?
flashcards.back: The material through which sound propagates; it can be a solid, a liquid or a gas.

flashcards.front: What did the ear-against-the-desk experiment show?
flashcards.back: The knock was heard through the table, showing that sound can also travel through solids.

flashcards.front: What is a vacuum?
flashcards.back: A space where there is no medium (matter) between the source of sound and the listener.

flashcards.front: Which three states of matter can carry sound?
flashcards.back: Solids, liquids and gases, as shown by the desk, the water and the air in the activities.

flashcards.front: What happens to the bell's sound as air is pumped out of the bell jar?
flashcards.back: It becomes fainter, and at near vacuum almost no sound is heard even though the bell is seen ringing.

flashcards.front: Why can astronauts not hear each other directly in space?
flashcards.back: Outer space is a near vacuum, so sound cannot propagate; they use special devices fitted into their spacesuits.

flashcards.front: What does the vacuum bell jar experiment prove?
flashcards.back: Sound cannot propagate in vacuum; it needs a medium, which may be a solid, a liquid or a gas.

flashcards.front: In which directions does sound propagate from a source?
flashcards.back: In multiple directions from the source; the directions may depend on the shape of the source.

flashcards.front: In the slinky activity, what do closely spaced and spread out regions represent?
flashcards.back: The higher or lower density of the air through which sound is travelling.

flashcards.front: Does the marked turn of the slinky travel along it?
flashcards.back: No. It only oscillates about its position of rest, parallel to the direction of the disturbance.

flashcards.front: Why do grains jump on the stretched sheet in Activity 10.6?
flashcards.back: The sound wave reaches the sheet and makes it vibrate, and this vibration moves the grains.

flashcards.front: What is sound a form of?
flashcards.back: Sound is a form of energy; a vibrating source transfers energy to the surrounding medium.

flashcards.front: What does a microphone do?
flashcards.back: It captures sound and converts sound energy to electrical energy as the wave passes through it.

flashcards.front: When a sound wave travels, what is actually transferred?
flashcards.back: Energy is transferred through particle vibrations and collisions, not the particles of the medium.

flashcards.front: What does the horizontal dashed line in the density-distance graph show?
flashcards.back: It marks the average density of the medium, above and below which the density varies.

flashcards.front: What is the crest of a sound wave?
flashcards.back: The highest point of the graph, representing the maximum density in a compression.

flashcards.front: What is the trough of a sound wave?
flashcards.back: The lowest point of the graph, representing the minimum density in a rarefaction.

flashcards.front: Which two ways can a sound wave be represented graphically?
flashcards.back: Density with distance at one instant, or density with time at one particular location.

flashcards.front: Define the wavelength of a wave.
flashcards.back: The distance between two consecutive crests or two consecutive troughs; symbol lambda, SI unit metre.

flashcards.front: Define the frequency of a sound wave.
flashcards.back: The number of density oscillations at a fixed point per unit time; SI unit per second, the hertz (Hz).

flashcards.front: Define the time period of a wave.
flashcards.back: The time taken for one complete density oscillation at a fixed point; symbol T, SI unit second.

flashcards.front: How are time period and frequency related?
flashcards.back: They are inversely related: T = 1/nu, so a shorter time period corresponds to a higher frequency.

flashcards.front: Which note has the lowest frequency among Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni?
flashcards.back: Sa is the lowest, and the frequency gradually increases for the other notes.

flashcards.front: Define the amplitude of a sound wave.
flashcards.back: The maximum change in the density of air in a compression or rarefaction compared to the average density.

flashcards.front: Define the intensity of sound.
flashcards.back: The amount of sound energy passing through a unit area perpendicular to the propagation direction in unit time.

flashcards.front: How are amplitude and energy of a wave related?
flashcards.back: A wave with a larger amplitude carries more energy than one with a smaller amplitude.

flashcards.front: Why does sound intensity decrease with distance from the source?
flashcards.back: The wave spreads over a larger area, so the same conserved energy is shared over a bigger area.

quiz.q: A tuning fork is usually made of which materials?
quiz.why: The book describes a tuning fork as a U-shaped metal bar usually made of steel or aluminium.

quiz.q: You touch a water surface with a vibrating tuning fork prong and see ripples. What does this prove?
options: The water vibrates on its own
quiz.why: Waves forming on the water surface indicate that the prongs of the tuning fork are indeed vibrating.

quiz.q: You hear a vibrating fork equally well in different orientations near your ear. What does this suggest?
options: Sound spreads in many directions from the source
Sound travels only along the fork's stem
The fork changes material when turned
Sound needs water to spread out
quiz.why: Hearing the sound in different orientations indicates sound propagates in multiple directions from the source.

quiz.q: In Activity 10.3, where do you place your ear to hear the desk knock through a solid?
quiz.why: With the ear against the desk, the sound is heard through the table, showing sound travels in solids.

quiz.q: While tapping submerged spoons, why must they not touch the sides or bottom of the bucket?
options: So the sound travels through the water
So the water does not spill
So the spoons do not rust
quiz.why: Touching the bucket would let the sound reach you through the solid bucket instead of through the water.

quiz.q: Sound reaches you from a source because it propagates through a
quiz.why: Sound propagates from its source to you through a medium, which may be a solid, liquid or gas.

quiz.q: In the bell jar experiment, what do you notice once near vacuum is reached?
options: The bell rings with almost no sound
The bell rings louder than ever
quiz.why: At near vacuum, almost no sound can be heard even though the bell can be seen ringing.

quiz.q: When air is let back into the bell jar, what happens to the sound?
options: It is heard again and grows as loud as before
quiz.why: With air back as the medium, the sound can be heard again and gradually becomes as loud as before.

quiz.q: Assertion: We cannot hear a bell in a jar after most air is pumped out. Reason: Sound requires a medium to travel.
options: Both true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both true, but R is not the correct explanation
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.why: Both statements are true, and the need for a medium explains why the sound fades in the jar.

quiz.q: In Activity 10.5, what travels from one end of the slinky to the other?
quiz.why: Disturbances created by push and pull move across the length of the slinky while the mark stays put.

quiz.q: In the slinky analogy, what do the bunched-up and spread-out turns stand for in air?
quiz.why: The closeness or spreading out of the turns represents the higher or lower density of air carrying sound.

quiz.q: Each slinky turn oscillates in place parallel to the disturbance. What does the air in a tube do likewise?
options: Particles oscillate about their own positions
Particles race along the whole tube
Particles pile up at one end
quiz.why: Like each turn of the slinky, air particles oscillate about their own positions while the disturbance travels.

quiz.q: Sound is a form of which quantity?
quiz.why: A vibrating source transfers energy to the surrounding medium as the sound wave propagates.

quiz.q: In Activity 10.6, the sound source never touches the sheet. Why do the grains still jump?
options: The sound wave makes the sheet vibrate
The grains are blown by wind
The beater throws grains from afar
The sheet vibrates on its own
quiz.why: As sound propagates through air it reaches the sheet and makes it vibrate, which moves the grains.

quiz.q: When sound travels from a tuning fork to your ear, what actually reaches your ear?
options: Energy carried by the sound wave
Air particles from near the fork
quiz.why: It is the energy that is transferred by the wave; the medium's particles only vibrate about their places.

quiz.q: In the density graph of a sound wave, which quantity is plotted on the x-axis?
quiz.why: Distance is plotted on the x-axis while the density of the medium is plotted on the y-axis.

quiz.q: Where on the density-distance graph would you find a rarefaction?
quiz.why: In the region of rarefaction the density falls below the average density, giving the lowest point.

quiz.q: The highest point of the density-distance graph represents which region?
quiz.why: The highest point is the crest, where the density of the medium is maximum in a compression.

quiz.q: What is the SI unit of wavelength?
quiz.why: Wavelength is a distance between consecutive crests or troughs, so its SI unit is the metre.

quiz.q: The unit hertz (Hz) measures which quantity?
quiz.why: Frequency has the unit per second, also called the hertz.

quiz.q: One complete density oscillation at a fixed point means
options: Maximum to minimum and back to maximum
Crest to the source and back
quiz.why: The change in density from maximum to minimum and again to maximum (or vice versa) is one complete oscillation.

quiz.q: A sound wave has a time period of 0.5 s. What is its frequency?
quiz.why: Frequency equals 1 divided by time period, so 1 over 0.5 s gives 2 Hz.

quiz.q: Why can a struck tuning fork make a nearly single frequency sound?
options: Its prongs oscillate steadily at one rate
quiz.why: The book notes that striking a tuning fork or oral whistling gives nearly single frequency sounds.

quiz.q: A larger change in density compared to the average corresponds to
quiz.why: A larger change in density in a compression or rarefaction corresponds to a larger amplitude.

quiz.q: In Activity 10.6, striking the plate harder makes the grains jump higher because
options: Air stops pressing on the sheet
quiz.why: A harder strike transfers more energy, so the sheet vibrates to a larger displacement and grains jump higher.

quiz.q: Two sounds leave the same point source with different amplitudes. Which travels farther before its intensity reduces to zero?
options: The one with larger initial amplitude
The one with smaller initial amplitude
Both fade at the same distance
quiz.why: Sounds with initial larger amplitude carry more energy and travel a larger distance before intensity reduces to zero.

examples.title: Finding frequency from time period
examples.problem: The density of air at a fixed point oscillates with a time period of 0.005 s as a sound wave passes. Find the frequency of the wave.
steps: Time period T is the time taken for one complete density oscillation at a fixed point; here T = 0.005 s.
Time period and frequency are inversely related by T = 1/nu, so nu = 1/T.
examples.answer: The frequency of the wave is 200 Hz.

examples.title: Reading wavelength from a graph
examples.problem: On a density-distance graph of a sound wave, one crest lies at 3 m on the distance axis and the next consecutive crest lies at 5 m. What is the wavelength of the wave?
steps: Wavelength is defined as the distance between two consecutive crests or two consecutive troughs.
The two consecutive crests are located at 3 m and 5 m on the distance axis.
Wavelength = 5 m minus 3 m = 2 m, which is the answer in the SI unit metre.
examples.answer: The wavelength of the wave is 2 m.

examples.title: Why the bell falls silent
examples.problem: An electric bell rings inside a bell jar while a vacuum pump slowly removes the air. Describe what you hear and see at near vacuum, and what happens when air is let back in.
steps: At first the bell rings inside the jar and the loudness of the sound is noted.
As air is sucked out using the vacuum pump, the sound becomes fainter because the medium inside thins out.
At near vacuum, almost no sound is heard even though the bell can be seen ringing, showing sound cannot propagate in vacuum.
When air is let back into the jar, the sound is heard again and gradually becomes as loud as before.
examples.answer: Sound needs a medium to propagate; at near vacuum the ringing bell is seen but almost not heard, and the sound returns as the air returns.

steps.label: Sources vibrate
steps.detail: Tuning fork prongs and other vibrating objects produce sound.

steps.label: Medium is a must
steps.detail: Solids, liquids and gases carry sound; a vacuum cannot, as the bell jar shows.

steps.label: Wave takes shape
steps.detail: Push and pull of the medium forms compressions and rarefactions, like slinky turns.

steps.label: Energy moves outward
steps.detail: Sound is energy; particles only oscillate while energy passes on through collisions.

steps.label: Draw the wave
steps.detail: A density-distance graph shows crests and troughs around the average density.

steps.label: Measure the wave
steps.detail: Wavelength, frequency and time period describe it, with T = 1/nu.

steps.label: Size up amplitude
steps.detail: Bigger density change means more energy, and intensity fades with distance.

steps.label: Gauge the speed
steps.detail: Sound propagates at a definite speed through each medium.

steps.label: Hear loudness and pitch
steps.detail: The ear experiences the physical wave as loudness and pitch.

steps.label: Reflect and apply
steps.detail: Echoes, reverberation, ultrasonic and infrasonic waves, and bat echolocation.
